issues.legal_issue: An unappealed interlocutory remand order that does not terminate the proceedings may be challenged in an appeal from the final order.
material_facts: The High Court remanded the tenants’ application after deciding that the statutory remedy remained available.
The landlords did not appeal the remand order.
After remand, the trial court rescinded the ejectment decree, and the landlords challenged that final order.
issues.conclusion: The landlords were not precluded from challenging the remand order’s ruling on the statutory remedy in their appeal from the final order.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata promotes finality, and under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure its principle may also apply between stages of the same proceeding. But a non-terminating interlocutory order can be challenged in an appeal from the final order; section 105 of the Code permits objections to interlocutory orders affecting the decision, subject to the special restriction in section 105(2) for an appealable remand order. The Court held that section 105(2) did not bar this challenge before it. It relied on Maharaja Mohesur Singh v. The Bengal Government, Forbes v. Amecroonissa Begum and Sheonath v. Ramnath, and distinguished Ramkripal Shukul v. Mst. Rup Kuari, Bani Ram v. Nanhu Mal and Hook v. Administrator General of Bengal, which concerned decisions that had effectively terminated earlier proceedings.

predicates.appeal_from_final_order: A party brought an appeal against the order that concluded the proceeding or its relevant stage.
predicates.challenged_order_did_not_terminate_proce: The earlier order was interlocutory and left the proceeding to continue toward a final decision.
predicates.no_appeal_lay_from_interlocutory_order: The earlier interlocutory order was not appealable.
predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_order_was_not_: Although an appeal from the earlier interlocutory order was available, the party did not take it.

issues.definition: When a party appeals a final order, it may challenge an earlier interlocutory order that did not terminate the proceedings if no appeal lay from that order or an available appeal was not taken.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory remedy omitted by an amendment is unavailable in proceedings to which the amendment applies, even if those proceedings began while the remedy was in force.
material_facts: The tenants applied under the original statute to have an ejectment decree rescinded, and that application remained pending when the relevant ordinance and amending statute took effect.
The amending statute omitted the provision that had authorized the application and provided that the amended statute applied to proceedings pending when the ordinance commenced.
The trial court rescinded the ejectment decree after the matter was remanded.
issues.conclusion: The omitted statutory remedy was unavailable in the pending proceeding, so the trial court acted without jurisdiction in rescinding the ejectment decree.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its decision in Mahadeolal Kanodia v. The Administrator-General of West Bengal, holding that section 28 of the original Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, after its omission by the amending Act, was unavailable in proceedings pending when the 1952 Ordinance commenced. The amended statute’s provision applying the amended law to those pending proceedings governed the matter.

predicates.statutory_tenancy_decree_rescission_proc: A party sought to rescind an ejectment decree by invoking a statutory tenancy remedy.
predicates.proceeding_pending_when_amendment_applie: The proceeding remained pending when the amended law was made applicable to it.
predicates.amendment_omitted_existing_rescission_re: The amendment applicable to the proceeding omitted the provision that had supplied the rescission remedy.

issues.definition: In a statutory tenancy decree-rescission proceeding, if the proceeding was pending when an amendment applied and that amendment omitted the existing rescission remedy, that former remedy is unavailable.
